title: Thermal Expansion of Liquids
short_intro: Thermal expansion of liquids is the fractional change in volume per unit change in temperature at constant pressure. Since liquids lack a definite shape, they exhibit only volume expansion characterized by real and apparent coefficients of expansion.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of real and apparent expansion of liquids, relation between coefficients (γ, γ<sub>r</sub>, γ<sub>a</sub>), expansion of vessels, and simple numerical problems on overflow of liquids.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed treatment of Dulong and Petit's method for determining real expansion, anomalous expansion of water, temperature dependence of coefficients, and differential expansion in complex manometric systems.

prerequisites: Thermal expansion of solids (linear, superficial, and volume expansion)
Equation of continuity and hydrostatic pressure

concept_notes.heading: Real and Apparent Expansion
bullets: When a liquid contained in a vessel is heated, both the vessel and the liquid expand simultaneously.
Real expansion (γ<sub>r</sub>) is the actual true expansion of the liquid per unit original volume per degree rise in temperature.
Apparent expansion (γ<sub>a</sub>) is the observed expansion of the liquid, uncorrected for the expansion of the container vessel.

concept_notes.heading: Relation Between Expansion Coefficients
bullets: The fundamental relation governing liquid expansion in a solid vessel is given by γ<sub>r</sub> = γ<sub>a</sub> + γ<sub>g</sub>, where γ<sub>g</sub> is the volume expansion coefficient of the glass or container vessel.
Since γ<sub>g</sub> = 3α<sub>g</sub> (where α<sub>g</sub> is the coefficient of linear expansion of the solid vessel), the relation becomes γ<sub>r</sub> = γ<sub>a</sub> + 3α<sub>g</sub>.
If γ<sub>a</sub> is positive, the liquid level rises upon heating; if it equals 3α<sub>g</sub>, the apparent expansion is zero.

concept_notes.heading: Anomalous Expansion of Water
bullets: Unlike most liquids that expand monotonically upon heating, water contracts when heated from 0°C to 4°C.
At 4°C, water possesses its maximum density of 1000 kg m<sup>-3</sup> (or 1 g cm<sup>-3</sup>).
This unique behavior is crucial for aquatic life survival in cold climates, as ice floats and bottom water remains at 4°C.

concept_notes.heading: Variation of Density with Temperature
bullets: As temperature increases, the volume of a given mass of liquid increases, causing its density to decrease according to the relation ρ<sub>t</sub> = ρ<sub>0</sub> / (1 + γΔt).
For small temperature changes, using the binomial approximation yields ρ<sub>t</sub> ≈ ρ<sub>0</sub> (1 - γΔt).
This temperature-induced density gradient is the primary driver of natural convection currents in fluids.

derivations.title: Relation Between Real and Apparent Expansion Coefficients
derivations.conditions: A liquid of initial volume V<sub>0</sub> is heated in a solid container of initial volume V<sub>0</sub> through a temperature rise ΔT.
steps: Let the initial volume of the liquid and the container be V<sub>0</sub> at temperature T<sub>1</sub>.
Upon heating to T<sub>2</sub> (where T<sub>2</sub> - T<sub>1</sub> = ΔT), let the true volume of the liquid become V<sub>L</sub> and the inner volume of the container become V<sub>C</sub>.
By definition of real expansion: V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>0</sub> (1 + γ<sub>r</sub>ΔT).
By definition of solid volume expansion: V<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>0</sub> (1 + γ<sub>g</sub>ΔT), where γ<sub>g</sub> = 3α<sub>g</sub>.
The apparent volume of the liquid overflow or observed volume in the graduated vessel is V<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> - V<sub>C</sub>.
Substituting the expressions: V<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>0</sub> (1 + γ<sub>r</sub>ΔT) - V<sub>0</sub> (1 + γ<sub>g</sub>ΔT) = V<sub>0</sub> (γ<sub>r</sub> - γ<sub>g</sub>)ΔT.
Since apparent volume is also defined as V<sub>a</sub> = V<sub>0</sub> γ<sub>a</sub> ΔT, equating both gives γ<sub>a</sub> = γ<sub>r</sub> - γ<sub>g</sub>.

derivations.title: Variation of Liquid Density with Temperature
derivations.conditions: Mass m of the liquid remains constant while temperature changes by ΔT.
steps: Mass of the liquid m = V<sub>0</sub>ρ<sub>0</sub> at initial temperature, where V<sub>0</sub> is initial volume and ρ<sub>0</sub> is initial density.
At final temperature T + ΔT, the volume becomes V = V<sub>0</sub> (1 + γΔT).
The final density ρ is given by ρ = m / V.
Substitute m = V<sub>0</sub>ρ<sub>0</sub> and V = V<sub>0</sub> (1 + γΔT) into the density equation.
Cancel V<sub>0</sub> from numerator and denominator: ρ = ρ<sub>0</sub> / (1 + γΔT).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Volume vs Temperature Graph for Water
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting volume (or specific volume) on the y-axis against temperature on the x-axis, showing a dip/minimum at 4°C.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The volume of a given mass of water decreases from 0°C to 4°C, reaching a minimum at 4°C, and increases for temperatures above 4°C, reflecting maximum density at 4°C.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT/PGT regarding why lakes freeze from top down and anomalous behavior interpretation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Dulong and Petit's Apparatus Principle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two vertical balanced liquid columns connected at the base by a horizontal tube, with one column maintained at 0°C in ice bath and the other heated to t°C in a steam/oil bath.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At hydrostatic equilibrium, the product of height and density remains constant: h<sub>0</sub>ρ<sub>0</sub> = h<sub>t</sub>ρ<sub>t</sub>. This allows precise determination of absolute liquid expansion without vessel interference.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct PGT theoretical questions on experimental determination of real expansion coefficient of mercury.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Apparent vs Real Expansion Demonstration
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A glass flask filled to the brim with colored liquid attached to a capillary tube, showing initial fall of liquid level followed by a continuous rapid rise upon heating.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The initial drop occurs because the glass flask expands first before heat reaches the liquid. The subsequent rapid rise represents the combined real expansion of the liquid exceeding the vessel expansion.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual multiple-choice questions explaining the apparent initial drop in liquid level.

solved_numericals.question: A glass vessel of volume 1000 cm<sup>3</sup> is filled completely with mercury at 0°C. What volume of mercury will overflow when the temperature is raised to 80°C? Given: coefficient of linear expansion of glass α<sub>g</sub> = 9 × 10<sup>-6</sup> K<sup>-1</sup> and coefficient of real expansion of mercury γ<sub>r</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>-4</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: V<sub>0</sub> = 1000 cm<sup>3</sup>, ΔT = 80°C, γ<sub>r</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>-4</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>, α<sub>g</sub> = 9 × 10<sup>-6</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.
Calculate volume expansion coefficient of glass vessel: γ<sub>g</sub> = 3α<sub>g</sub> = 3 × (9 × 10<sup>-6</sup>) = 2.7 × 10<sup>-5</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.
Calculate apparent expansion coefficient of mercury: γ<sub>a</sub> = γ<sub>r</sub> - γ<sub>g</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>-4</sup> - 0.27 × 10<sup>-4</sup> = 1.53 × 10<sup>-4</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.

solved_numericals.question: The density of a liquid at 0°C is 1.06 g cm<sup>-3</sup> and its coefficient of real expansion is 0.00021 K<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate its density at 100°C.
solution_steps: Identify given data: ρ<sub>0</sub> = 1.06 g cm<sup>-3</sup>, γ = 0.00021 K<sup>-1</sup>, ΔT = 100°C - 0°C = 100 K.

solved_numericals.question: A solid of density 5000 kg m<sup>-3</sup> is weighed in a liquid whose coefficient of real expansion is 8 × 10<sup>-4</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>. If the temperature of the system is raised by 20 K, find the percentage change in the apparent weight of the solid, ignoring the expansion of the solid.
solution_steps: Apparent weight W' = Actual Weight (W) - Upthrust (F<sub>u</sub>).
When temperature increases by ΔT, the liquid density changes as ρ<sub>T</sub> = ρ<sub>0</sub> / (1 + γΔT) ≈ ρ<sub>0</sub> (1 - γΔT).
Since solid expansion is ignored, V<sub>solid</sub> remains constant, meaning Upthrust F<sub>u</sub> becomes F<sub>u</sub>' = F<sub>u</sub> (1 - γΔT).

Since apparent weight decreases when upthrust increases, percentage change in apparent weight depends on the relative magnitude. The fractional change in upthrust is γΔT = 8 × 10<sup>-4</sup> × 20 = 0.016 or 1.6%.
solved_numericals.answer: 1.6% decrease in apparent weight (increase in upthrust)

assumptions_and_limitations: Coefficients of expansion (γ and α) are assumed to be constant over moderate temperature ranges (ΔT < 100°C).
Container vessels are assumed to be isotropic and undergo uniform homogeneous expansion.
Pressure is assumed constant during thermal expansion experiments unless explicit compressibility effects are integrated.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Liquids have only one coefficient of thermal expansion like solids.
common_misconceptions.correct: Liquids exhibit both real and apparent coefficients of expansion because the container holding the liquid also expands.
common_misconceptions.why: The observed expansion of a liquid depends entirely on the expansion properties of the vessel used to contain it.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Water expands continuously as temperature is lowered to freezing point.
common_misconceptions.correct: Water contracts from 4°C to 0°C due to anomalous expansion, reaching maximum density at 4°C.
common_misconceptions.why: Hydrogen bonding and cage-like molecular structuring in cold water cause volume to increase despite cooling.

common_misconceptions.wrong: When a heated liquid-filled vessel is first placed in a heat source, the liquid level immediately rises.
common_misconceptions.correct: The liquid level initially drops before rising.
common_misconceptions.why: The solid container receives thermal energy first and expands, increasing its internal volume before the heat reaches the liquid inside.

quick_revision: Real expansion of liquid equals the sum of apparent expansion and volume expansion of the container: gamma_r = gamma_a + 3 alpha_g.
Water has maximum density and minimum volume at exactly 4°C.
Density of a liquid decreases inversely with temperature rise according to rho = rho_0 / (1 + gamma Delta T).
